events.description:
We propose a half-day Agentic Football Cup hackathon during Boston AI Week 2026 — a proven, globally-run AWS workshop (100+ events, rated 4.8/5) where participants build a squad of five autonomous AI agents using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and the Strands Agents SDK, then compete in live 5v5 AI football matches on a real-time leaderboard. Participants write the strategy; their agents play the match. Five autonomous AI agents per team make decisions every two seconds — passing, shooting, pressing, and defending — with no human input once the whistle blows. This isn't a demo you watch; it's a working system you build and deploy in an afternoon.

Every 2 seconds, the game server emits a decision point and calls all 10 agents in parallel with the full game state. Each agent has 1 second to return one of eleven structured commands:
```
MOVE_TO | PASS | SHOOT | DRIBBLE | PRESS_BALL | MARK | INTERCEPT | TACKLE | CLEAR | IDLE | (GK actions)
```
Miss the deadline → your player IDLEs for that tick. The match doesn't pause. This hard latency contract mirrors real production agentic workloads. The thing participants tune is almost never the code — it's the prompt and the model choice:
-   System prompt encodes team tactics ("press high, favor through-balls, shoot from distance")
-   Model selection balances reasoning depth vs. latency budget
-   Structured output schema bounds the action space

Teams of 2–4 (form on-site or pre-register)    
-   No AI/ML experience needed — the workshop is designed for developers of all levels
-   Non-technical teammates welcome (naming the squad, picking formation, trash talk)

Every team that completes the workshop qualifies for the Agentic Football Cup global league. Group winners fly to Las Vegas to compete live on stage at AWS re:Invent. events.description: Public debate about artificial intelligence runs along two tracks: whether deployment is outpacing our ability to govern it, and when systems will match general human capability. That pattern may be the predictable behavior of a functioning market applied to a technology with large positive externalities, meaning that capability improvements alone may not correct it. I'll introduce a framework for reasoning about return per unit of compute, a model of where human conceptual work retains economic value without any appeal to human superiority, and what AI's gold-medal Mathematical Olympiad performance does and doesn't establish. events.title: AI Governance: The Difference Between a Pilot and a Successful Rollout
events.notesCa: Importat automàticament d'aiweek.boston/schedule (extracció 2026-09-13). Text de seu original: "venue TBA".
events.description:
Most enterprise AI initiatives don't fail in the lab — they fail in production, when nobody can say with confidence what data trained the model, who has access to it, or what happens when it gets something wrong.
A pilot only has to work once, in a controlled environment, in front of a friendly audience. A rollout has to work every time, at scale, under regulatory scrutiny, with real customer data flowing through it. Governance is what closes that gap: it's the difference between a demo that impressed the board and a system the board is willing to bet the company on.
Without it, most AI programs stall at the same point — legal won't sign off, security can't trace the data lineage, and the pilot quietly gets shelved. With it, the questions that normally kill a rollout get answered before they're ever asked: What data trained this? Who's accountable if it's wrong? Can we prove that to a regulator?

events.description:
Every company already has a brain. It is just spread across inboxes, CRM notes, shared drives, and the memory of whoever has been there the longest. The knowledge already exists. The work is connecting it.

Join Unosquare for a candid panel on designing a company brain: infrastructure that gathers an organization's scattered knowledge and relationships into one place it can actually query, without depending on the one person who happens to remember. The idea looks different on every desk. A law firm surfaces a judge's prior rulings in seconds instead of an afternoon. A recruiter notices when a hiring manager moves and the relationship travels with them. A private equity team pulls comparable deals to pressure-test the one in front of them. Underneath, it is the same system.

We will get into the design decisions that make or break it: separating raw source material from the refined knowledge built on top, treating relationships as records with a date, a source, and a confidence level, and governing how information earns its way to institutional truth. Promotion is a decision, not a default, and a company brain is only as trustworthy as the sources it can point back to. Along the way, we will be honest about where AI earns its place: turning search into synthesis, conversation into records, and volume into signal.

This is not a feature you switch on; it is infrastructure. Whether you are a founder deciding if the investment is worth making, an engineer weighing memory architectures, or a designer trying to make trust visible in an interface, come with questions. events.title: Training Custom AI Models via Fine-Tuning
events.notesCa: Importat automàticament d'aiweek.boston/schedule (extracció 2026-09-13). Text de seu original: "Location TBA".
events.description:
This talk is a practical introduction to creating a custom AI model through fine-tuning. Rather than training a model from scratch, I will show how you can start with an existing open-weight model and specialize it to behave in a specific, repeatable way. The focus will be on the complete workflow: choosing a base model, defining the behavior you want to change, creating synthetic training data, establishing evaluation benchmarks, and fine-tuning with techniques such as LoRA and QLoRA.

I will also cover the parts of the process that are easy to overlook, including quantization, controlling variables during evaluation, checking for catastrophic forgetting, and measuring whether the fine-tuned model actually improved instead of simply assuming that it did. The goal is to demystify fine-tuning and show, step by step, how an open model can be turned into a specialized model that can be evaluated, deployed, and used in a real application.

events.notesCa: Importat automàticament d'aiweek.boston/schedule (extracció 2026-09-13). Text de seu original: "Virtual".
events.description:
What if the biggest risk of AI isn't what it gets wrong about you, but whether it sees you at all?

A qualified candidate never makes the shortlist.
A neighborhood disappears from the recommendations.
A small business loses customers it never knew were looking.
A community organization never reaches the funder searching for exactly what it does.

No rejection. No notification. No obvious moment when something went wrong.

You simply weren't in the answer.

A year apart on the TEDxRoxbury stage, Shana Feggins and Angela Pitter came at this from opposite ends.

Shana Feggins, in Rewriting AI's Future for All, looked at the people behind the machine: who builds AI, whose perspectives shape its choices, and what happens when human blind spots make their way into systems increasingly used for hiring, lending, healthcare, and other consequential decisions. Her warning: AI has no morals. Humans do.

Angela Pitter looked beneath it, at the information AI has to work with. Her talk, AI and Digital Erasure: The New Redlining We're Not Talking About, asks what happens when the people, businesses, and whole communities AI should know about are missing, poorly represented, or difficult for these systems to find and verify.

They ended up asking the same question:
Who does AI see, who does it leave out, and what happens when you're missing from the answer?

Sometimes AI has information about you and gets the story wrong. Sometimes the evidence it needs to see you clearly isn't there. As AI increasingly shapes what gets discovered, recommended, and funded, that difference matters.

For Boston AI Week, Shana and Angela bring these two ideas together for the first time.

This isn't a replay of two talks. It's a live conversation, followed by open Q&A.

Join us on Zoom to be in the room: ask your question, share what you're seeing, or just listen in.
Prefer to watch? We'll stream live on LinkedIn and bring questions from the comments into the conversation.

Bring the example that makes you wonder: Does AI actually see the world I know?

AI orchestration in 2026 looks a lot like programming in 1952: hand-tuned prompts, model-specific quirks, and all the bookkeeping left to the developer.
